title: Finding an initial basic feasible solution

sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 260 200" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>the first quadrant</title><line x1="48" y1="168" x2="236" y2="168"/><polygon points="236,168 229.6,170.7 229.6,165.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="48" y1="180" x2="48" y2="24"/><polygon points="48,24 50.7,30.4 45.3,30.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="230" y="184" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="56" y="20" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><rect x="48" y="48" width="150" height="120" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.10"/></svg>
sections.body_md:
The simplex iteration needs a basic feasible solution to start from. A slack basis is feasible only when the right-hand side is nonnegative. A general standard-form system need not offer that basis. Phase I builds an auxiliary linear program whose feasible set is easy and whose optimal value answers the feasibility question.

First write the constraints as equalities and multiply any row with a negative right-hand side by \(-1\), so that \(b \ge 0\). Then add a nonnegative artificial variable to each row, and minimize the sum of the artificial variables. The original cost is ignored. The artificial columns form an identity basis, and \(a = b\) is a basic feasible solution of the auxiliary problem.

Run the ordinary simplex iteration on that auxiliary problem. If the optimal auxiliary value is positive, no point of the original system exists: every original feasible point would have given the artificials the value zero. If the optimal auxiliary value is zero, the artificials are zero at the optimal basis, and dropping them leaves a basic feasible solution of the original program. Phase II then restores the original cost and continues from that basis.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
With \(b \ge 0\), phase I is
\[
\text{minimize } \sum_i a_i \quad \text{subject to } Ax + a = b,\ x \ge 0,\ a \ge 0.
\]
At the artificial basis the reduced cost of an original column with entries \(a\) and \(b\), in a two-row problem, is \(-a - b\). The original system is feasible if and only if the auxiliary optimal value equals 0. A positive optimal value is a certificate of infeasibility, and the certificate does not depend on the original cost.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Consider \(x + y \ge 6\) and \(2x + y \ge 20\), with \(x, y \ge 0\). After surpluses and artificials, the rows are \(x + y - s + a = 6\) and \(2x + y - t + r = 20\). The artificial basis has objective \(6 + 20\).

The dock artificial is 26. The column of \(x\) is \((1, 2)\), so its phase-I reduced cost is \(-3\), and the ratios are \(6/1\) and \(20/2\). The step is 6. One further pivot drives the remaining artificial to zero and leaves the feasible point \(x = 10\), \(y = 0\). The original system is feasible, and this point is a legal start for the original objective. The original costs were never used.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: A positive value at the artificial basis is not infeasibility. It is only the starting value. Infeasibility is a positive value at optimality. A second miss is to fold the original cost into the auxiliary objective. A pivot can then trade a worse artificial sum for a better original cost and stop at a point that is not feasible for the original system. A third is to forget the sign flip on a negative right-hand side. The artificial basis \(a = b\) is feasible only when \(b \ge 0\).

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: With a feasible basis in hand, the original reduced costs take over and the simplex iteration optimizes the cost that the modeler actually cares about. The same standard form is the starting point for the dual linear program, read off from multipliers on the equalities. Other algorithms for linear programs, built from scaled quadratic models or from a perturbed system of equations, assume the same feasible region and do not need this auxiliary basis as their first step.
